query: Which GLP-compatible repeat-dose toxicity endpoints, contaminant thresholds, and study durations are required now for IND-readiness versus later bridge studies?

response.query: Which GLP-compatible repeat-dose toxicity endpoints, contaminant thresholds, and study durations are required now for IND-readiness versus later bridge studies?
response.answer: For IND-readiness, GLP-compliant repeat-dose toxicity studies of at least 28 days in rodents and non-rodents are required. Longer studies may be needed for later bridge studies, depending on clinical trial duration. Regulatory guidance suggests studies should match or exceed clinical trial duration.

results.title: From Molecule to IND | WuXi AppTec
results.content: Before advancing to clinical trials, regulatory authorities require comprehensive safety data to support an Investigational New Drug (IND) application. This guide outlines the essential study categories needed for IND submission, detailing their objectives, required endpoints, and how they contribute to the safe and efficient transition to human trials. * Metabolite identification (Met ID) studies to evaluate species differences and human relevance. Dose Range Finding (DRF) & Non-GLP Tolerability Studies: Optimizing Safety Before GLP. These studies are conducted to evaluate how animals tolerate different doses of the compound before starting GLP-compliant toxicology. A DRF study is particularly important because it identifies appropriate dose levels and potential target organ effects, helping to inform the design of repeat-dose GLP studies. **Key non-GLP and DRF studies include:**. * DRF studies (often 7–14 days) in both rodent and non-rodent species. * Repeat-dose tolerability (3- to 7-day studies). These studies reduce risk and cost by revealing early toxicity, avoiding dose missteps in GLP studies, and informing species selection. GLP Toxicology Studies: Establishing the Safety Profile. GLP (Good Laboratory Practice) toxicology studies are the regulatory cornerstone for evaluating drug safety prior to clinical trials. * 28 repeat-dose toxicity studies in rodents and non-rodents. According to ICH S7A/S7B, safety pharmacology studies are required to evaluate whether your compound interferes with essential functions such as heart rate, respiration, or nervous system activity. Once all required studies are complete, the focus turns to organizing the data into a structured IND submission that supports initiation of clinical trials. * Final GLP study reports and bioanalytical validations. By taking a strategic approach to how ADME, DRF, toxicology, and safety data are generated, you can improve regulatory clarity and development efficiency. results.title: Repeat Dose Toxicity Testing • WuXi AppTec Lab Testing Division
results.content: # Repeat Dose Toxicity Testing. Repeat dose or chronic toxicity studies help evaluate the effects of repeat administration of a new drug candidate over a defined period of time. Chronic toxicity studies help you select proper dosing amounts for GLP studies and identify potential target organs affected by the compound. As an experienced partner in general toxicology testing, WuXi AppTec can help you build a safety assessment program that includes the correct repeat dose toxicity studies for your needs. ## Repeat Dose Toxicity Testing Capabilities. WuXi AppTec offers end-to-end toxicology testing for all stages of the drug development lifecycle, including IND-enabling, subchronic, and chronic repeat dose studies. ## Repeat Dose Toxicity Study Species & Routes of Administration. Our experienced team can help you design repeat dose toxicity studies with the right toxicological species, dose level, routes of administration, analyses, and regulatory support. Repeat dose chronic toxicity studies are part of a complete general toxicology program. ## Repeat Dose Toxicity Data. Repeat dose toxicity studies generate data that deepen researchers’ understanding of dose and toxicity for a given compound. This chronic toxicity data helps identify correct dosing for the pivotal later stage GLP studies. Repeat dose toxicity studies are a critical part of the drug development lifecycle, playing important roles through the discovery, preclinical to IND, and clinical stages. ## Repeat Dose Toxicity Study Durations. The U.S. FDA’s “M3(R2) Nonclinical Safety Studies for the Conduct of Human Clinical Trials and Marketing Authorization for Pharmaceuticals” provides guidance on the recommended length of repeat dose toxicity studies. ## Explore Related Resources About Repeat Dose Toxicity & General Toxicology Testing. #### Repeat Dose Toxicity: 3 Possible Timeframes for Your IND-Enabling Studies. ## Repeat Dose Toxicity Studies FAQ. ### What are repeat dose toxicity studies? Repeat dose toxicity studies test the safety of a new drug candidate by exposing animals to repeated doses of the compound and monitoring for signs of toxicity over the course of 14-28 days. ### Why are repeat dose toxicity studies necessary? Repeat dose toxicity studies evaluate the effects of repeat administration over a defined period of time. ### How do repeat dose toxicity studies add value to my testing program? The repeated-dose toxicity studies are essential for the quantitative risk assessment of drug molecules.

results.title: Repeat Dose Toxicity Study - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: The durations of the repeat-dose toxicity studies should depend on the indication and the length of the proposed clinical trial and should be at least equal to that of the clinical trial (usually a minimum of 2 weeks) in accordance with the ICH Guidance M3 (R2) Nonclinical Safety Studies for the Conduct of Human Clinical Trials for Pharmaceuticals [42]. However, if the target organ profile is similar across species and/or similar class effects are observed and the dose selected in the clinical trials appears acceptable, then chronic toxicity studies in a single species may be justifiable to reduce animal use. For chronic use products, repeat-dose toxicity studies of 6 months’ duration using rodents or nonrodents are considered sufficient, providing the high dose is appropriately selected; studies of longer duration have not generally provided useful information that changed the clinical course of development. The EMA currently recommends at least one repeat-dose toxicity study in a relevant species (e.g. rat) of at least four weeks duration that includes a comprehensive evaluation of TK and characterization of ADAs. This study ideally would be conducted with the formulation intended for clinical use and the dosage form, strength, and route of administration should match the intended clinical paradigm. Drugs more often than not require longer term (than four weeks of dosing) clinical trials than these to reach market (ICH E8, and M3) which means that longer term (than the typical 28-day IND enabling repeat dose toxicity studies) must be conducted in both selected rodent and non-rodent species, particularly as one moves towards late Phase 2 clinical studies where larger numbers of patients are exposed for longer durations, usually with less direct patient oversite. In traditional INDs, single-dose studies are conducted in at least 2 mammalian species (typically 1 rodent and 1 nonrodent species) by the intended clinical route of administration and designed to evaluate clinical observations (including local tolerance), toxicokinetics, hematology, clinical chemistry, necropsy data, and histopathology data after a single administration, with further evaluations conducted 2 weeks postexposure to assess for the occurrence of delayed toxicity and/or recovery.

results.title: Repeat Dose Toxicity: 3 Possible Timeframes for Your IND-Enabling Studies
results.content: # Repeat Dose Toxicity: 3 Possible Timeframes for Your IND-Enabling Studies. **Repeat dose toxicity studies evaluate the effects of repeat administration over a defined period of time. Toxicity data from repeat dose studies helps researchers deepen their understanding on the potential target organs of toxicity, exposure, and potential toxic effects of a compound. The duration of repeat dose toxicity studies must be informed by the duration, indication, and scope of your clinical plan while staying in the bounds of regulatory guidance. The U.S. FDA’s “M3(R2) Nonclinical Safety Studies for the Conduct of Human Clinical Trials and Marketing Authorization for Pharmaceuticals” outlines recommended duration of repeat dose toxicity studies. In general, toxicity studies must be conducted in one rodent and one non-rodent species with a duration that is equal to or exceeds the duration of the human clinical trial. ## 3 Repeat Dose Toxicity Study Durations. The FDA says that acute studies in 2 species “for a minimum duration of 2 weeks would generally support any clinical development trial up to 2 weeks in duration.” Maximum Tolerated Dose (MTD) studies fall into this category, which are used to determine the highest dose tolerated over multiple doses. There are many options for completing these acute repeat dose toxicity studies to get an idea for how a subject will respond after multiple doses – whether you start with a single dose across a few subjects or multiple dose levels across a few subjects. The goal is to escalate to where you get clinical observations that would prohibit that dose from being used over repeated time frames in future studies. Typically, a 28-day study is conducted to support clinical dosing. Depending on the clinical dosing regimen, you may need a follow-up 13-week study. While acute studies help you determine if subjects can tolerate a dose level over a shorter time period, sub-chronic studies start to get more complex. Generally, 6-month rodent and 9-month non-rodent studies support clinical dosing for trials over 6 months. In fact, you can’t design your toxicity studies without an estimate of the dose level and dosing schedule planned for the clinic. This plan will inform selection of the dose levels needed for your toxicity studies.

results.title: Repeat Dose Toxicity Study - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Repeat dose toxicity studies are defined as toxicological assessments conducted over multiple doses and durations, typically including pilot studies and chronic studies in two species (rodents and non-rodents), to evaluate the safety and potential adverse effects of a substance prior to human clinical trials. In principle, the duration of the animal toxicity studies should be equal to or exceed the duration of the human clinical trials, up to the maximum recommended duration of the repeat dose toxicity studies. Recommended Duration of Repeat Dose Toxicity Studies to Support the Conduct of Clinical Trials. The objective of repeat-dose toxicity studies is to evaluate adverse effects of compounds when administered to the experimental animals repeatedly for a period of time. When new drug candidates are tested in repeat-dose toxicity studies, it is common for the animals in the mid- and high-dose groups to show altered function of certain organs, abnormal blood chemistry or hematology, or abnormal urine analysis during the course of the study. By the time a new chemical is considered for chronic toxicity studies, information has already been collected regarding the chemical-induced toxicities in animals, including target organs, toxic dose levels, and degree of toxicities in acute, short-term, and subchronic toxicology studies. Therefore, early resolution of this question, i.e., in the 28-day repeat dose general toxicity studies, requires consideration of the regulatory region(s) intended for marketing approval, and appropriate animal age selection and study design. The purpose of repeat-dose toxicity studies is to determine the effects of repeated administration of the vaccine/adjuvant in animals. For vaccines intended to be given repeatedly in the clinic, the number of doses administered to the animals in repeated-dose toxicity studies should equal or exceed the number of doses proposed in humans. However, if the target organ profile is similar across species and/or similar class effects are observed and the dose selected in the clinical trials appears acceptable, then chronic toxicity studies in a single species may be justifiable to reduce animal use (Chapman et al., 2012; ICHS6(R1)). The EMA currently recommends at least one repeat-dose toxicity study in a relevant species (e.g. rat) of at least four weeks duration that includes a comprehensive evaluation of the effects on blood coagulation and hemostasis.
